key_terms.meaning: Speech is a source from the lungs and vocal folds passed through the vocal tract filter.
Periodic vibration of the vocal folds that produces voiced sounds such as vowels.
The pharynx, mouth and nasal cavities that filter the glottal source.
The point in the vocal tract where airflow is narrowed or blocked for a consonant.
How airflow is blocked, narrowed or released for a consonant, such as stop or fricative.
A smallest sound unit that distinguishes words in a language.
Fourier transform of a short windowed frame of speech.
A time-frequency picture made by stacking frame magnitude spectra.
A short speech segment, often 20 to 30 ms, assumed roughly stationary.
A frequency band within which the ear's filters interact strongly.
A perceptual frequency scale that is roughly linear below 1 kHz and logarithmic above it.
Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, a short feature vector from log mel spectra.
Speech coding and feature method that predicts each sample from past samples.
A model with hidden states and observable acoustic emissions used for speech recognition.
Dynamic programming search for the most probable hidden state path.
A probability model P(W) over word sequences used to rank recognition hypotheses.
Text-to-speech that joins recorded speech units to form an utterance.
Patterns of pitch, duration, energy and pauses that shape spoken delivery.
Cycle-to-cycle variation in fundamental frequency, used as a voice-quality measure.
Cycle-to-cycle variation in amplitude, used as a voice-quality measure.

takeaways: Speech production is a source-filter system: lungs supply air, vocal folds switch voicing and the vocal tract filters the sound.
Sampling turns the source and the slowly changing vocal-tract filter into discrete-time signals.
Every speech sound belongs to a place and manner class, with voicing as a third major contrast.
Speech is nonstationary, so analysis uses short frames and the short-time Fourier transform.
A spectrogram shows how the frequency content of speech changes over time.
The ear uses overlapping critical bands, so Mel or Bark scales suit speech features better than a linear frequency axis.
MFCCs and linear prediction compress a frame, while speech codecs compress the waveform by discarding what the ear may not miss.
HMM recognition chooses W = argmax P(X|W)·P(W), combining acoustic evidence with a language prior.
Text-to-speech reverses recognition: text to phonemes, a prosody plan, then a waveform by rules or recorded units.
Emotion recognition uses utterance-level pitch, energy, pause, speaking-rate, jitter and shimmer statistics.
bank_note: Long answers usually stress the source-filter model, place and manner of articulation, short-time analysis and spectrograms, HMM recognition with the argmax rule, and rule-based versus concatenative synthesis.

bank.q: Explain human speech production using the source-filter model. Show how it becomes a discrete-time model after sampling.
outline: Lungs supply air; vocal folds switch voicing on and off.
Vocal tract acts as a slowly changing filter.
Voiced source is periodic; unvoiced source is noisy.
Sampling gives a discrete source signal driving a discrete filter.
Frame-by-frame analysis assumes the filter changes slowly.

bank.q: Explain place and manner of articulation. Give one example each for stop, fricative and nasal sounds.
outline: Place is where the tract narrows: bilabial, alveolar, velar and so on.
Manner is how airflow is blocked, narrowed or released.
Stops block and release airflow.
Fricatives force air through a narrow gap.
Nasals route air through the nasal cavity.
Voicing is an independent contrast.

bank.q: Why is short-time Fourier analysis used for speech? Define frame, window and spectrogram.
outline: Speech changes with time, so a single global spectrum is not enough.
Split speech into short frames, often 20 to 30 ms.
Apply a window such as Hamming to reduce leakage.
Take the Fourier transform of each frame.
Stack magnitude spectra over time to form a spectrogram.

bank.q: Describe critical bands and the Mel scale. Why are they used in speech features?
outline: The ear analyses sound in overlapping frequency bands.
Critical bands describe this limited frequency resolution.
Mel and Bark scales give a perceptual frequency axis.
Features on a Mel scale match hearing better than linear frequency bins.

bank.q: Describe the MFCC extraction pipeline for one frame of speech.
outline: Pre-emphasise the signal.
Frame and window the speech.
Compute the Fourier transform magnitude.
Apply a Mel filterbank and take logs.
Apply the discrete cosine transform.
Keep the low-order cepstral coefficients.

bank.q: Apply an HMM to isolated-word speech recognition. Define states, transition matrix, emission model and Viterbi decoding.
outline: Hidden states represent phones or word parts.
Transition matrix gives state-to-state probabilities.
Emission model gives P(frame|state).
Viterbi finds the most probable state path.
Word identity comes from the best matching HMM.

bank.q: Given a trained acoustic model and a language model, explain the argmax rule for speech recognition. Include word boundary detection.
outline: Use Bayes rule to write P(W|X) proportional to P(X|W)·P(W).
P(X|W) is the acoustic likelihood from the HMM.
P(W) is the language-model prior.
Search for W that maximises the product.
Word boundaries come from the lexicon and segmentation path.

bank.q: Describe rule-based and concatenative text-to-speech synthesis from text input to waveform.
outline: Normalise text and expand numbers and abbreviations.
Convert text to phonemes.
Build a prosody plan for pitch, duration and pauses.
Rule-based synthesis generates parameters by rules.
Concatenative synthesis selects and joins recorded units.
Smooth joins and modify prosody before output.

bank.q: Explain how to extract and classify emotion from speech using pitch, energy, pause length and speaking rate.
outline: Compute frame-level pitch and energy.
Measure pauses and speaking rate over the utterance.
Add jitter and shimmer for voice quality.
Summarise with mean, variance and range.
Train a classifier on labelled utterances.

bank.q: Compare MFCC and LPC features for speech recognition.
outline: MFCCs model perceptual mel-scale spectral shape.
LPC models the vocal-tract filter directly.
MFCCs are common in recognition; LPC is common in coding.
Discuss dimensionality, robustness and computation.
Note that both lose phase and fine detail.

bank.q: Analyze how an HMM continuous speech recogniser combines acoustic frames, pronunciation and language model. Discuss two failure modes.
outline: Context-dependent phone states model acoustic frames.
Pronunciation lexicon links phones to words.
Language model ranks word sequences.
Search keeps partial hypotheses and applies pruning.
Failure modes include noise mismatch and language-model bias.

bank.q: Evaluate concatenative versus parametric or rule-based text-to-speech for naturalness, footprint and flexibility.
outline: Concatenative speech is natural in covered contexts.
It needs a large recorded database.
Parametric speech is compact and flexible.
Parametric speech may sound buzzy or less natural.
Choose by domain, memory budget and voice flexibility.

bank.q: Evaluate the use of jitter, shimmer and prosodic statistics for emotion recognition. Note confounds.
outline: Emotion is carried by prosody and voice quality.
Jitter and shimmer measure voice irregularity.
Pitch, energy and rate statistics summarise an utterance.
Speaker, language and recording channel can confound labels.
Report normalisation and evaluation protocol.

bank.q: Trace a complete speech pipeline from waveform to text and back to waveform. Identify shared representations and where information is lost.
outline: Waveform is produced by the source-filter system.
Short-time analysis gives frames and spectrograms.
Features such as MFCCs compress each frame.
HMM recognition uses argmax P(X|W)·P(W).
TTS maps text to phonemes, prosody and waveform.
Coding and feature extraction discard information irreversibly.

glossary.def: A model that gives P(X|W), the likelihood of acoustic feature sequence X for a word or phone sequence W.
The argument that maximises a function, written argmax, as in choosing W that maximises P(X|W)·P(W).
A perceptual frequency scale based on critical bands.
A search that keeps only the few best partial hypotheses at each step.
The inverse Fourier transform of the log magnitude spectrum, used to separate source and filter effects.
A coder-decoder pair that compresses speech for storage or transmission.
Frame-to-frame differences that add local dynamics to a static feature vector.
A resonance peak of the vocal tract visible as a dark band in a spectrogram.
The repetition rate of voiced speech, perceived as pitch and measured in hertz.
A set of triangular filters spaced on the Mel scale.
Text-to-speech that generates speech from a compact model rather than joining recorded units.
The study of speech sounds, their production, transmission and perception.
The perceived highness of a voice, related to fundamental frequency.
A first-order high-pass filter that boosts high frequencies before speech analysis.
Concatenative synthesis that chooses recorded units from a database to match a target context.
A system that analyses speech into parameters and resynthesises it from those parameters.
Finding where one word ends and the next begins in a continuous speech signal.
A measure of signal strength, often the sum of squared sample values in a frame.
The duration of silence or near-silence between speech segments.
The number of syllables, words or phones spoken per unit time.
Dividing a speech signal into short overlapping segments for analysis.
A taper such as Hamming applied to a frame to reduce spectral leakage.
A transform that converts log mel spectrum values into decorrelated cepstral coefficients.
The probability of an observed acoustic frame given a hidden HMM state.
